elevations.tip: Pound each chicken breast between plastic wrap to an even ¾-inch thickness, then dry-brine with kosher salt for 30 minutes before breading. For the breading, mix ⅓ cup finely grated Pecorino Romano into the panko and toast the panko in a dry skillet with 2 tablespoons olive oil until golden BEFORE dredging — this way the crust is already crispy and just needs to set in the oven.
elevations.why: Even thickness means every bite cooks at the same rate — no dry edges or raw center. Dry-brining seasons the meat throughout. Pre-toasting panko means you can finish in a hot oven instead of shallow-frying, and the crust arrives shatteringly crispy rather than soggy under the sauce.

elevations.tip: Make a quick San Marzano sauce: crush a 28-oz can by hand (no blender — you want texture), simmer with 3 smashed garlic cloves, a pinch of red pepper flake, and a torn basil stem for 20 minutes. Finish with 1 tablespoon cold butter swirled in off-heat and a shower of torn fresh basil leaves.
elevations.why: Hand-crushed tomatoes give you irregular, jammy pockets of sauce that cling to the crust. The butter adds body and a subtle richness that rounds the acidity. Fresh basil at the end keeps its bright, peppery perfume — cooked basil turns muddy.

elevations.tip: Use a two-cheese approach: a thick blanket of low-moisture mozzarella melted under the broiler until blistered and spotty, then immediately top with torn pieces of fresh burrata or fresh mozzarella so it barely melts into a creamy layer on contact.
elevations.why: The low-moisture mozz gives you that stretchy, browned cheese crust everyone loves. The fresh cheese on top adds a cool, milky richness that contrasts with the hot, crispy chicken underneath. Two textures of the same ingredient — it's a chef move that reads as luxurious.

name: Grilled Chicken with Lemon and Herbs

elevations.tip: Spatchcock the chicken (or use bone-in thighs) and marinate for at least 2 hours in a mixture of ½ cup full-fat Greek yogurt, zest of 2 lemons, 4 smashed garlic cloves, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 1 teaspoon cumin, 1 teaspoon smoked paprika, and a big pinch of salt. The yogurt tenderizes without making it mushy.
elevations.why: Yogurt marinades are the secret weapon of Middle Eastern and Indian grilling — the lactic acid gently breaks down surface proteins for incredibly tender meat, while the yogurt's fat carries flavor deep into the flesh. The slight char on yogurt-marinated chicken is unmatched.

elevations.tip: While the chicken rests, make a 2-minute salsa verde: roughly chop a big handful each of parsley and mint, mix with 2 tablespoons capers (chopped), 1 minced garlic clove, juice of 1 lemon, red pepper flakes, and enough olive oil to make it spoonable. Spoon it over the carved chicken at the table.
elevations.why: Grilled chicken needs a bright, herbal counterpoint to cut through the smoky richness. This salsa verde is the restaurant trick that makes people say 'what IS that?' — the capers add briny pops, the mint lifts everything, and the raw garlic gives it backbone.

elevations.tip: Serve the chicken hot off the grill but pair it with a cold, crunchy shaved fennel and arugula salad dressed with lemon juice, olive oil, shaved Parmesan, and flaky salt.
elevations.why: Hot protein against a cold, crisp salad creates the kind of sensory contrast that makes a simple Monday dinner feel like a composed restaurant plate. The anise note in fennel is a classic pairing with lemon chicken.

elevations.tip: Finish the pasta in the sauce: pull the pasta from the boiling water 90 seconds early (while still chalky in the center), transfer directly into the sauté pan with your sauce and ½ cup starchy pasta water. Toss vigorously over medium heat for 60-90 seconds — the starch emulsifies with the fat and creates a glossy, clingy sauce that coats every strand.
elevations.why: This is the single most important technique in Italian pasta cooking. The starch in the pasta water acts as a natural emulsifier, binding the sauce to the noodle. You'll never have a puddle of sauce at the bottom of the bowl again. Quick, no extra time — just a change in when you drain.

elevations.tip: Keep it fast — brown 4 tablespoons butter in a light-colored pan until it smells nutty and the solids turn amber (about 3 minutes). Immediately toss in a handful of fresh sage leaves — they'll crackle and crisp in 10 seconds. Pour this over the finished pasta with a squeeze of lemon and a blizzard of Parmigiano.
elevations.why: Brown butter and sage is the classic pairing for egg-yolk pasta because the nutty, toasty butter amplifies the richness of the yolks while the sage adds an earthy, almost savory-sweet note. The lemon squeeze at the end is the secret — it cuts through the richness and makes the dish sing. Total time: 4 minutes.

name: Corned Beef Hash with Yellow Potatoes

elevations.tip: The cardinal rule of hash: DO NOT STIR. Get your cast-iron skillet ripping hot with a mix of butter and oil. Spread the potato-and-corned-beef mixture in an even layer and press it down firmly with a spatula. Let it sit untouched for 5-6 minutes until the bottom develops a dark, crackling crust. Flip in sections (not all at once) and repeat.
elevations.why: Hash isn't a sauté — it's a crust-building exercise. That undisturbed contact with the screaming-hot pan creates a golden, shatteringly crispy bottom that contrasts with the tender, salty meat inside. Stirring is the enemy of texture here.

elevations.tip: Top each serving with a fried egg (crispy edges, runny yolk) and a generous spoonful of quick-pickled red onions: thinly slice 1 red onion, toss with ½ cup apple cider vinegar, 1 tablespoon sugar, and a pinch of salt. Let sit 20 minutes while you cook. The pink, tangy onions cut right through the richness.
elevations.why: Corned beef hash is gloriously rich and salty — it needs acid and brightness to balance. The runny egg yolk becomes a built-in sauce, and the pickled onions add a vinegary snap and gorgeous color. This is the diner trick that separates great hash from heavy hash.

elevations.tip: Par-boil the yellow potatoes (cut into ½-inch cubes) for exactly 6 minutes — until a knife meets slight resistance. Drain and let them steam dry in the colander for 5 minutes. The roughed-up edges from the parboil will crisp beautifully in the skillet.
elevations.why: Raw potatoes in hash take forever and cook unevenly. Par-boiling gives you a head start, and the starchy, roughed-up surface area is what creates maximum crunch when it hits the hot fat. Dan can get this going the minute he walks in with Elsie.

name: Grilled Steaks with Potatoes, Peppers, and Cilantro Chimichurri

elevations.tip: Reverse-sear the steaks: salt them heavily 1 hour before cooking. Set up a two-zone grill — indirect heat on one side, blazing coals on the other. Cook the steaks on the cool side with the lid on until the internal temp hits 115°F (about 20-25 minutes for 1.5-inch steaks). Then move to the searing-hot side for 60-90 seconds per side until you get a dark, mahogany crust. Rest 10 minutes.
elevations.why: At 87°F outside, you've got a hot grill working in your favor. Reverse-searing gives you edge-to-edge medium-rare with a crust that rivals a steakhouse. The low-then-high approach dries the surface, which means better Maillard browning. This is the single biggest upgrade you can make to a grilled steak.

elevations.tip: Make chimichurri that punches: 1 cup packed cilantro (stems and all), ½ cup packed parsley, 4 garlic cloves, 1 minced serrano chile (seeded for Elsie's portion), ¼ cup red wine vinegar, ¾ cup olive oil, 1 teaspoon dried oregano, and flaky salt. Pulse in a food processor — leave it chunky, not smooth. Make it 30 minutes ahead so the flavors meld.
elevations.why: Chimichurri is the Argentinian steak sauce for a reason — the raw garlic and vinegar cut through beef fat, the herbs add freshness, and the olive oil carries it all. Using cilantro as the lead herb instead of the traditional parsley-heavy version gives it a more vibrant, punchy character that pairs with the peppers.

elevations.tip: Grill the peppers and potatoes (halved baby potatoes, tossed in oil and salt) directly on the grates alongside the steak during the searing phase. Serve the sizzling-hot vegetables with the cold chimichurri spooned over everything at the table.
elevations.why: Hot, smoky, slightly charred vegetables meeting bright, cold, acidic chimichurri — this is the contrast that makes outdoor grilling feel like an event, not just dinner. The potatoes get a crust from the grill grates that no oven can match.

elevations.tip: Crank your oven as high as it goes (500-550°F) with a baking steel or inverted sheet pan on the lowest rack for at least 45 minutes before baking. If you have a pizza stone, even better. Stretch the dough on a well-floured peel and work fast — the key to a blistered, charred crust is maximum heat from below. Each pizza should take only 6-8 minutes.
elevations.why: Most home pizza fails because the oven isn't hot enough. A preheated steel conducts heat far better than a cold sheet pan, giving you the leopard-spotted char and puffy cornicione (edge crust) of a pizzeria. This single change transforms home pizza.

elevations.tip: Offer three creative no-pork pizzas: (1) Spicy Chicken & Roasted Red Pepper — shredded rotisserie chicken, roasted red peppers, thin red onion, mozzarella, finished with hot honey drizzle and fresh basil. (2) White Pizza with Ricotta & Greens — dollops of ricotta, garlic oil base (no red sauce), sautéed spinach or arugula added after baking, lemon zest, black pepper, and shaved Parm. (3) Margherita Plus — San Marzano sauce, fresh mozzarella, fresh basil, but add torn pieces of burrata after baking and a drizzle of really good olive oil.
elevations.why: Three distinct pizzas give guests variety and make it feel like a pizza party, not just pizza night. The hot honey on the chicken pizza is the unexpected hit that everyone will talk about. The white pizza is elegant. The Margherita Plus with burrata is indulgent. Zero pork, zero compromise.

elevations.tip: Serve a simple arugula salad alongside: baby arugula, shaved Parmesan, lemon juice, good olive oil, flaky salt. Toss it at the last second so the arugula stays perky. For Elsie, add some cherry tomatoes and a milder dressing.
elevations.why: Pizza is rich, cheesy, and carb-heavy — a peppery, lemony arugula salad is the classic Italian counterpunch. It cleanses the palate between slices and makes the whole meal feel balanced rather than heavy.

name: Grilled Smash Burgers with Green Goddess Salad

elevations.tip: Use 80/20 ground beef (chuck). Season only the outside — mix salt, pepper, and garlic powder, then press it onto the formed patties' surfaces rather than mixing into the meat. Form patties slightly wider than your buns and press a thumbprint dimple in the center. Grill over high direct heat: 4 minutes first side (don't touch), flip once, add cheese immediately, close lid for 2 minutes to melt.
elevations.why: Mixing seasoning into burger meat compacts it into a hockey puck — you're making a meatloaf at that point. Surface seasoning keeps the interior loose and juicy while building a savory crust. The dimple prevents the burger from puffing into a ball. One flip only — every flip costs you crust.

elevations.tip: Make a quick smash-style burger sauce: ¼ cup mayo, 2 tablespoons ketchup, 1 tablespoon yellow mustard, 2 tablespoons finely diced dill pickles, 1 teaspoon pickle brine, a pinch of garlic powder, and a few dashes of hot sauce. Also: toast the buns cut-side down on the grill for 30 seconds — this is non-negotiable.
elevations.why: A great burger sauce ties everything together and adds moisture. The pickle brine is the secret ingredient — it adds a tangy depth that makes people ask what's different. Toasted buns create a barrier against burger juice so the bottom bun doesn't disintegrate. This is the difference between a backyard burger and a great backyard burger.

elevations.tip: Upgrade the Green Goddess salad dressing: blend 1 avocado, ½ cup buttermilk, a big handful each of basil, chives, and tarragon, 2 anchovy fillets (trust me — they add savory depth, not fishiness), juice of 1 lemon, 1 garlic clove, salt and pepper. Toss with crisp Little Gem or romaine, shaved cucumber, snap peas, and radishes. Top with toasted pepitas for crunch.
elevations.why: Green Goddess from a bottle is fine. Green Goddess made fresh with real herbs and avocado is a revelation — creamy, bright, herbaceous, and it turns a side salad into something people eat with a spoon. The toasted pepitas add a nutty crunch that plays off the creamy dressing. At 88°F, this cold salad will be the hero of the meal.
